title: TB4-11154
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX (hereinafter called the P.A.), and his spouse, XXXXX, both citizens of the Ukraine, are appealing the decisions of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), denying their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants have submitted new evidence in support of their appeals and they are requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division find them to be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

This appeal is allowed. Pursuant to Section 111 (1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers this claim to the Refugee Protection Division for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel with directions to examine the "new" evidence and properly canvass the issue of Internal Flight Alternative, as articulated below. Background:
The Appellants' claims are based on their ability to practice their religion as Baptist Christians, without placing their lives in danger.

They began to attend the Church of Evangelical Baptists Christians at the invitation of their son in the middle of 2009. In September 2010, the Appellants were baptized. Because of their strong beliefs, the Appellants, wherever possible, attempted to spread the gospel to neighbours, people on the street and in the workplace. However, in August 2010, the P.A.'s husband was dismissed from his workplace, after only a few weeks. According to the P.A., management did not like the fact that he had been spreading the word of God in the workplace.

In February 2013, the P.A.'s husband (the Appellant) secured a position in the XXXX. He and the P.A. decided to ask management to provide them with a room with a swimming pool where new members of their church could be baptized. Management agreed to their request, however, during one of their baptism events, the inspectors, from the head office, arrived and the Appellant was fired as a result.

In November 2013, new neighbours moved into the Appellants' building. When they found out that the Appellants were Baptists, they began to insult their faith. In December 2013, a door of their apartment was vandalized and they wrote a denunciation to the police. The police indicated that they would investigate. In January 2014, the P.A.'s husband faced the neighbour and the tension worsened, culminating in the neighbour beating the P.A.'s husband. On this occasion, the Appellants knew for certain the identity of the perpetrator, however, according to the P.A., the police did not believe them. The police, according to the P.A., advised them that they would be better off to stop preaching the heresy and leave the sect, and then life would improve.

The Appellants learned at their church that others were being attacked. They attempted to sell their apartment, but had difficulty given the poor economy. Then they found, suspended on a rope, a piece of meat with a note "soon we will have all the sectarians hanged." The Appellants decided not to go to the police as they had done nothing previously. They and their son decided that the best way out of the situation was to temporarily visit their daughter in Canada. They decided that once things calmed down, they would return to the Ukraine, sell their possessions and move to another location within the Ukraine.

Meanwhile, in Canada, the Appellants continued to chat online with family members and they saw that the Acting President of Ukraine is a Baptist and that this fact had been widely discussed, which, in turn, divided the society of the Ukraine into two parts. ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL EXPRESS STATUTORY CONDITIONS

Section 110(4) of IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of his claim or that was not reasonably available, or that he could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

If the statutory requirements have been met, the panel must then consider the factors in Raza,1 in which the Federal Court of Appeal set out factors to be considered in assessing "new" evidence. While Raza predates the introduction of IRPA, Section 110(4), it is based on the very similar wording of Section 113(a) for the PRRA (Pre-Removal Risk Assessment). The Court held that new evidence should be considered for its newness, credibility, relevance, and materiality, in addition to any express statutory provisions.

The Appellants have submitted a significant amount of "new" evidence. However, in light of the RAD's decision, it is not necessary to assess the admissibility of these documents. The RAD suggests that the Appellants forward these documents as soon as a "de novo" (new) hearing is scheduled with the RPD. ROLE OF RAD:

A recent Federal Court decision in Huruglica2 has provided the RAD with guidance on the role of the RAD. Justice Phelan states, in paragraphs 54 and 55, of the foregoing decision. 54. Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. 55. In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."

While there has been some conflict in the case law from the Federal Court regarding the standard of review to be applied by the RAD, when reviewing RPD decisions, Justice Martineau in Alyafi3 has said that, in the face of this conflict, the Federal Court should allow the RAD to apply either approach as long as the question of the scope of the appellate review of the RPD's decisions has not been settled by a final judgment by the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada. The RAD has applied the reasoning as set out in Huruglica. SUBMISSIONS BY APPELLANTS:
Given that the Appellants are unrepresented, the RAD accepts their statement as a Memorandum of Argument in support of their appeal. RAD'S FINDINGS:
The RAD has examined the RPD's decision in which "Internal Flight Alternative" (IFA) was considered to be the determinative issue.

The RAD has found that the RPD erred in applying the "IFA" test. Firstly, with respect to the first prong of the IFA test, the RPD has not provided a clear analysis of how these claimants would meet the first prong of the IFA test, although it is addressed partially under the second prong. However, more importantly, the RPD has not provided any analysis of the second prong whatsoever, yet has stated that an IFA to Kyiv is not objectively unreasonable. The RAD finds that this constitutes an error in law. The RAD would be able to conduct an independent assessment of the first prong, however, in the absence of any evidence to support the second prong, the RAD is unable to substitute a decision.

This appeal is allowed. Pursuant to Section 111 (1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers this claim to the Refugee Protection Division for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel.
